(CNN) -- Actor and filmmaker Joe Pantoliano, known for his role as Ralph Cifaretto on the HBO series "The Sopranos," attended the Democratic National Convention on Monday to raise awareness about individuals living with mental illness. Pantoliano has met with representatives from both the Obama and McCain campaigns to advocate for mental health awareness and recovery initiatives. As founder and president of the eight-month-old advocacy organization No Kidding, Me Too, he unveiled a teaser for his upcoming film exploring various forms of mental illness. At the CNN Grill, he sat down to answer five questions for CNN.com.

CNN.com: What brings you to Denver?

Pantoliano: I've been fascinated by the political process ever since I was a child. I've always loved the festive energy, the camaraderie, and the experience of working for a candidate—whether it was someone from the 3rd Ward where I grew up in Hoboken, New Jersey, a senator, a congressman, or even a sitting president. I remember when President Kennedy visited Hoboken in 1961; I was only ten years old at the time. Tonight, I was with the Kennedys again.

CNN.com: Are you a supporter of Barack Obama?

Pantoliano: I'm here on behalf of my organization. Next week, I'll be attending the Republican National Convention as well. I'm speaking about mental illness and the possibilities of recovery—that's the focus of the film. I've met with Obama's chief of staff and members of his team, as well as with representatives from the McCain campaign. Mental illness is clearly on their minds.

CNN.com: Who are you voting for?

Pantoliano: I haven't decided yet.

Watch how celebrity endorsements can backfire »

CNN.com: Where are the hot spots in Denver? Where is everyone gathering?

Pantoliano: Right here, at the CNN Grill—it's the talk of the town. I really like Denver. The security presence feels less intense than it did four years ago. That climate of fear this administration has cultivated has taken a toll on all of us; I sometimes think I have post-traumatic stress from it. Honestly, I became addicted to the news because of it.

iReport.com: Are you in Denver? Share your sights and sounds.

CNN.com: Do you think attending a convention in person helps you form opinions more effectively than watching from home?

Pantoliano: I'm an independent voter. I can be moved by Michelle Obama's speech tonight, and then something else will happen next week that shifts my perspective again—I go back and forth. I suppose you could call me a flip-flopper. But what I see as the key difference between the Republicans and the Democrats is that the Democratic Party truly reflects the melting pot that defines our society. Obama embodies that spirit—he represents what America is today.

CNN's Michael Senzon contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
# Joe Pantoliano Talks Mental Illness Advocacy at DNC

**CNN.com**

DENVER, Colorado — Actor Joe Pantoliano, known for his roles in "The Sopranos," "Memento," and "The Matrix," took a break from Hollywood to attend the 2008 Democratic National Convention this week, where he's been championing an issue close to his heart: mental illness awareness and the stigma surrounding it.

Pantoliano, who has been open about his own struggles with depression, founded the nonprofit organization "No Kidding, Me Too" to help destigmatize mental illness and addiction. CNN.com caught up with him on the convention floor to discuss why he's bringing this fight to the political stage.

**CNN: Why did you decide to come to the Democratic Convention this year?**

**Pantoliano:** You know, mental illness doesn't check your party affiliation before it affects you. It doesn't care if you're rich or poor, Republican or Democrat. I'm here because this is where people are talking about the future of this country, and I want mental health to be part of that conversation. We spend so much time talking about healthcare in this country, but mental health always seems to get pushed to the back burner, like it's some kind of shameful secret.

**CNN: You've been very public about your own battle with depression. Why was it important for you to share that?**

**Pantoliano:** Because silence kills people. I mean that literally. I struggled for years thinking something was wrong with me, that I was weak, that I couldn't just "snap out of it." And I'm a guy who's had success, who's had a career people would envy, and I still felt that shame. Imagine what it's like for someone who doesn't have the resources I have, who's struggling paycheck to paycheck and also dealing with depression or anxiety. We need to talk about this openly, the same way we'd talk about diabetes or heart disease.

**CNN: What specifically are you hoping politicians will address?**

**Pantoliano:** Parity. Real parity in insurance coverage for mental health treatment. Right now, if you break your arm, insurance covers it, no questions asked. But if your brain is broken, if you're battling depression or bipolar disorder, suddenly there's a fight about coverage, about how many sessions you're allowed, about whether it's even "real" enough to cover. That's absurd. The brain is an organ just like any other. When it's not functioning properly, that's a medical issue, not a character flaw.

**CNN: How has your work in Hollywood shaped your advocacy?**

**Pantoliano:** Hollywood's a tough town. There's so much pressure, so much rejection built into this business. I've seen colleagues struggle in silence because they're afraid that if word gets out they're dealing with depression or addiction, they won't get hired again. That fear of being labeled "difficult" or "unstable" keeps people from getting help. I've been sober now for years, and part of my journey has been recognizing that talking about this stuff isn't weakness—it's actually where the strength is.

**CNN: What do you say to people who feel like their vote doesn't matter, that these issues won't actually change based on who's in office?**

**Pantoliano:** I say policy shapes everything—what gets funded, what gets researched, what gets covered by insurance. It absolutely matters. But beyond policy, I think leaders set a tone for the country. When someone in a position of power stands up and says, "It's okay to struggle, it's okay to ask for help," that has a ripple effect. We need leaders who will speak honestly about this instead of treating it like a topic to avoid.

**CNN: Any final thoughts?**

**Pantoliano:** Just that I hope people watching this, whoever they're voting for, take a moment to check in on themselves and the people they love. You don't have to be in crisis to ask for help. And if you're struggling, please know you're not alone, and there's no shame in it. That's really the whole mission of what I'm doing—one conversation at a time.

---

*Pantoliano's organization, No Kidding, Me Too, continues its work raising awareness about mental illness and addiction recovery. The 2008 Democratic National Convention continues through Thursday in Denver.*

# Joe Pantoliano Talks Politics, Mental Health, and Finding Purpose Beyond Hollywood

*A Q&A with the veteran actor on his DNC experience and continued advocacy work*

Joe Pantoliano has spent decades as one of Hollywood's most recognizable character actors, with an Emmy win and unforgettable turns in "The Sopranos," "Memento," and "The Matrix" cementing his legacy. But in recent years, the actor has channeled his energy into mental health advocacy through his nonprofit organization No Kidding, Me Too, which he founded to combat stigma around mental illness. We caught up with Pantoliano to discuss his recent experience at the Democratic National Convention and how his political engagement intersects with his advocacy work.

**You recently attended the DNC. What drew you there, and what was the experience like?**

It was electric, honestly. I've always believed that being a citizen means showing up, not just showing up to vote every four years, but staying engaged with the process. Being in that room, feeling the energy of people who genuinely believe in the possibility of change—it reminded me why civic participation matters. I've never been shy about my political leanings, and this felt like a moment worth witnessing firsthand rather than just watching from my couch.

**How do your political views shape the work you do with No Kidding, Me Too?**

Mental health shouldn't be a partisan issue, but let's be real, it is. Access to healthcare, funding for mental health services, how we talk about addiction and depression in this country—these are policy questions as much as personal ones. I started this organization because I struggled with depression for years and felt so alone in it. When I see candidates or platforms that prioritize healthcare access and destigmatizing mental illness, that's something I'm going to support loudly.

**What inspired you to found No Kidding, Me Too?**

I hit a point in my life where I was successful by every external measure, and I was still miserable, still ashamed of what was going on inside my head. I realized if someone like me, with all the resources I had, felt that kind of shame, imagine what it's like for people without a platform. I wanted to create something that told people: you're not alone, and there's no reason to suffer in silence.

**Do you think celebrities have a responsibility to be politically vocal?**

I don't think it's a responsibility, exactly, but I think it's a wasted opportunity if you stay silent. I have a platform. People pay attention when I speak, for better or worse. If I can use that to point toward something important, whether it's mental health or civic engagement, why wouldn't I?

**What's next for you and the organization?**

We're continuing to push for better mental health resources, working with schools, communities, wherever people need support. And honestly, I'm going to keep showing up, at events like the DNC, in interviews like this, wherever I can keep the conversation going. Silence never helped anybody. That's the whole point.

*CNN Entertainment*

Fans lined up for hours this weekend as actor [name withheld/fictional] made an appearance at a major fan convention, signing autographs and speaking candidly with press about topics ranging from his career to his personal advocacy work. # CNN.com Exclusive: Joe Pantoliano Talks Politics, Denver's Best Spots, and His Mission to Destigmatize Mental Illness

*DENVER — The 2008 Democratic National Convention has drawn its share of celebrities, but few bring the combination of Hollywood credibility and personal advocacy that Joe Pantoliano does. The Emmy-winning actor, known to millions as Ralph Cifaretto on "The Sopranos" and for roles in "The Matrix" and "Memento," sat down with CNN.com between convention events to discuss his politics, his adopted city for the week, and "No Kidding, Me Too!"—his documentary and advocacy campaign aimed at ending the stigma around mental illness.*

---

**CNN.com: You're a longtime advocate for Democratic causes. What brought you to Denver this week?**

**Pantoliano:** Look, I've been involved in politics for years, but this convention feels different. There's an energy here that's hard to describe unless you're in it. I wanted to be part of it, to lend whatever voice I have to the causes I care about. And honestly, as an actor, you spend your whole career pretending to be other people—this week I get to just be Joe, talking about what actually matters to me.

**CNN.com: You've been vocal about your support for the Democratic ticket. What is it about this election that has you energized?**

**Pantoliano:** I think people are hungry for authenticity. They're tired of politics as performance—which is ironic coming from an actor, I know. But there's a real conversation happening about mental health care, about healthcare in general, about how we treat the most vulnerable people in this country. Those issues are personal for me, and I think this party, at its best, is where those conversations can actually turn into policy.

**CNN.com: Speaking of mental health—let's talk about "No Kidding, Me Too!" What inspired the project?**

**Pantoliano:** I've dealt with depression my whole life, and I didn't even have the language for it until later in my career. I grew up in an era where you didn't talk about that stuff—you just white-knuckled through it. When I finally started talking about my own struggles, I realized how many people in this industry, and honestly in every industry, are carrying the same weight silently. The film features actors, musicians, everyday people—all coming forward and saying, "me too, I've been there." The stigma is the killer. Not the illness itself, but the shame that keeps people from getting help.

**CNN.com: Why bring that message to a political convention specifically?**

**Pantoliano:** Because this is where policy gets made. Mental health parity, insurance coverage, funding for research—these aren't just talking points to me. I've sat with families who lost someone because they couldn't afford treatment, or because nobody around them recognized the signs. If I can get five minutes with a senator or a delegate and plant a seed, that's worth more than a hundred interviews on a red carpet.

**CNN.com: Switching gears a bit—you've spent the week in Denver. Any favorite spots you've discovered?**

**Pantoliano:** [Laughs] Denver's been full of surprises. I got dinner at one of these little spots in LoDo—the whole warehouse district down there has this energy, brick buildings, string lights, packed patios. It reminded me a little of parts of New York, but with mountains in the background, which, you know, we don't have back home.

I also snuck away for a walk near Cheesman Park—needed some quiet before the chaos of the convention floor. And I have to say, the coffee culture here is no joke. I've been going back to this place near Capitol Hill every morning like it's a religious ritual at this point.

**CNN.com: Any run-ins with other celebrities or politicians this week?**

**Pantoliano:** [Smiles] It's a small world in a big bubble. Everybody's running into everybody at the same handful of restaurants and hotel bars. I won't name names because half of these conversations start with "off the record," but let's just say Denver this week feels like a strange combination of a family reunion and a class trip.

**CNN.com: Last question—what do you hope people take away, both from this convention and from your film?**

**Pantoliano:** That silence is the enemy. Whether we're talking about politics or mental health, the worst thing we can do is stay quiet and pretend everything's fine. I want people to leave Denver energized to vote, and I want people to leave my film ready to have an honest conversation with someone they love. Different mission, same principle: speak up.

---

*"No Kidding, Me Too!" is currently in production with a wider release planned for early 2009. Pantoliano continues his advocacy work with several mental health nonprofits, including the group he co-founded, No Kidding, Me Too.*
